name: Facial Artery Musculomucosal (FAMM) Flap

dominant_pedicle.artery: Facial artery (inferiorly based antegrade or superiorly based retrograde via angular artery)
dominant_pedicle.veins: Submucosal buccal venous plexus (facial vein often lies posterior to flap)

perforators.label: Facial Artery Buccal Perforators
perforators.location: Along oblique line from retromolar trigone toward alar base
perforators.relation_to_landmarks: Course just deep to buccinator and anterior to Stensen duct papilla

vascular_anatomy.venous_drainage_notes: Relies on intact submucosal venous plexus along a 1.5–2 cm mucosal base; skeletonizing the artery alone risks venous congestion.
vascular_variants: Prior neck dissection with facial artery ligation precludes inferiorly based harvest

motor: Buccal branches of facial nerve lie just deep to buccinator — stay on deep muscular plane carefully

dimensions.thickness_notes: Thin, pliable, hairless, mucus-secreting mucosal lining ideally matching oral cavity defects.

arc_of_rotation.pivot_point: Retromolar trigone (inferiorly based) or gingivolabial sulcus (superiorly based)
arc_of_rotation.reach_description: Inferiorly based reaches floor of mouth, ventral tongue, and lower alveolus; superiorly based reaches hard palate, upper alveolus, and nasal septum.

indications: Floor of mouth and ventral tongue defects
Palatal fistula and anterior skull base/nasal lining
Lip vermilion and alveolar ridge reconstruction
contraindications: Prior ipsilateral facial artery ligation (for inferiorly based)
Dentition biting across pedicle without bite block or extraction
advantages: Like-with-like mucosal replacement without hair or external skin scar
Rapid single-stage or minor pedicle-division staging
disadvantages: Limited width (~3 cm)
Potential pedicle compression by molar teeth requiring bite block or second-stage division

donor_site.closure: Primary mucosal closure if ≤2.5–3 cm; buccal fat pad advancement or healing by secondary intention if wider.
morbidity: Risk of Stensen duct injury if posterior margin is not preserved

technique.patient_positioning: Supine with nasal intubation and mouth gag.
preoperative_planning: Map facial artery intraorally with handheld Doppler
Identify and protect Stensen duct papilla opposite upper 2nd molar
technique.design: Oblique 2.5–3 cm wide mucosal island centered over Doppler facial artery path anterior to Stensen duct.
harvest_steps: 1. Mark Stensen duct papilla and Doppler trace facial artery along buccal mucosa.
2. Incise distal tip first to identify and ligate distal facial artery cleanly.
3. Elevate mucosa, submucosa, and thin buccinator cuff while keeping facial artery attached to deep surface.
4. Preserve 1.5–2 cm mucosal/submucosal base for venous outflow and inset without tension.
pearls: Identify the facial artery distally first at the superior or inferior tip before committing both sides of the flap.
pitfalls: Injuring Stensen duct or skeletonizing the artery without submucosal venous cuff.

recipient_vessels_options: Pedicled axial flap on facial artery

references.book: Pribaz J et al. Plast Reconstr Surg (FAMM Flap)

name: Submental Artery Island Flap
tissue_components: Optional ipsilateral anterior belly of digastric

dominant_pedicle.veins: Submental vein draining to common facial / anterior jugular vein

perforators.label: Submental Perforators
perforators.location: Inferior border of mandible near anterior belly of digastric
perforators.relation_to_landmarks: Course deep or superficial to anterior belly of digastric (~70% deep)

vascular_anatomy.venous_drainage_notes: Preserve common facial vein confluence; reverse-flow modification possible for upper face if facial vessels intact distally.
vascular_variants: Submental artery runs deep to anterior belly of digastric in ~70% of dissections — include anterior belly of digastric to safeguard pedicle

motor: Marginal mandibular branch of facial nerve (at risk near facial vessels — identify and preserve)
nerves.donor_numbness_note: Submental numbness; contour often improves neck profile.

dimensions.thickness_notes: Thin, pliable, excellent facial skin color and texture match; beard hair in male patients requires caution for oral cavity.

arc_of_rotation.pivot_point: Facial artery takeoff beneath submandibular gland
arc_of_rotation.reach_description: Reaches oral cavity, tongue, floor of mouth, lower/midface, cheek, and lower lip.

indications: Oral cavity / hemiglossectomy reconstruction when free flap is contraindicated or rapid OR time desired
Lower and midfacial cutaneous resurfacing (ideal color match)
Pharyngeal / palatal defects
contraindications: Clinically positive Level IA/IB nodal metastases (oncologic contraindication)
Prior facial vessel ligation
advantages: Excellent facial color/texture match
Concealed submental scar with aesthetic necklift effect
Shorter OR time than RFFF
disadvantages: Risk of marginal mandibular nerve palsy
Hair-bearing intraoral paddle in men
Oncologic concern in N+ level I neck

donor_site.closure: Primary closure in submental crease (pinch test preoperatively).

preoperative_planning: Perform pinch test to confirm primary submental closure
Confirm N0 status in Level IA/IB on imaging
technique.design: Transverse ellipse from angle to angle just beneath mandibular border.
harvest_steps: 1. Incise superior border ~1.5 cm below mandible and identify marginal mandibular nerve.
2. Elevate from contralateral side in subplatysmal plane toward ipsilateral anterior belly of digastric.
3. Include ipsilateral anterior belly of digastric and mylohyoid cuff to protect submental vessels.
4. Skeletonize facial vessels proximally if extra pedicle reach is needed and tunnel into oral cavity or cheek.
pearls: Routine inclusion of the ipsilateral anterior belly of digastric prevents inadvertent pedicle injury.
pitfalls: Harvesting in patients with occult Level IB nodal disease.

references.book: Martin D et al. Plast Reconstr Surg (Submental Island Flap)

name: Temporalis Muscle Flap

classification.mathes_nahai: Type III (anterior & posterior deep temporal arteries)

dominant_pedicle.artery: Anterior and posterior deep temporal arteries
dominant_pedicle.artery_origin: Second part of internal maxillary artery
dominant_pedicle.veins: Deep temporal veins draining to pterygoid venous plexus

minor_pedicles: Middle temporal artery (from superficial temporal artery)
vascular_anatomy.venous_drainage_notes: Dual anterior/posterior deep temporal supply allows sagittal splitting of the muscle into anterior and posterior halves.
vascular_variants: Pedicles enter the deep medial surface just superior to the coronoid process

motor: Deep temporal nerves (V3 mandibular division of trigeminal nerve)
nerves.donor_numbness_note: Temporal hollowing contour deformity unless reconstructed with implant/fat/posterior muscle advancement.

dimensions.thickness_notes: Fan-shaped muscle ~8–12 cm wide, well-vascularized myofascial surface that mucosalizes rapidly inside oral/palatal defects.

arc_of_rotation.pivot_point: Coronoid process / infratemporal fossa (releasing zygomatic arch increases reach by 2–3 cm)
arc_of_rotation.reach_description: Reaches orbit, maxilla, hard/soft palate, retromolar trigone, lateral skull base, and oral commissure (facial reanimation).

indications: Maxillectomy and palatal defect obliteration (mucosalizes spontaneously)
Orbital exenteration cavity obliteration
Dynamic facial reanimation (orthodromic temporalis tendon transfer / Labbé lengthening myoplasty)
Skull base and TMJ interposition
contraindications: Prior ipsilateral internal maxillary artery ligation or sacrifice
High-dose infratemporal irradiation risking necrosis
advantages: Exceptionally reliable dual deep vascular supply
Spontaneous intraoral mucosalization without skin graft
Allows dynamic smile reanimation
disadvantages: Visible temporal hollowing donor deformity
Risk to frontal branch of facial nerve during zygomatic arch osteotomy
Moderate trismus

donor_site.closure: Hemicoronal scalp incision closed primarily; consider MEDPOR/PEEK implant or posterior muscle transposition to fill temporal hollow.
donor_site.functional_loss: Minimal mastication loss if contralateral temporalis and masseters are intact.

preoperative_planning: Confirm internal maxillary artery patency on CT/MRI
Plan temporal contour reconstruction if full muscle is transferred
technique.design: Hemicoronal incision preserving superficial temporal vessels in scalp flap; harvest entire muscle or split anterior/posterior.
harvest_steps: 1. Elevate scalp flap deep to superficial temporal fascia (preserving frontal branch within TPF).
2. Incise pericranium along superior temporal line and strip temporalis subperiosteally off temporal bone.
3. Protect anterior and posterior deep temporal pedicles on deep surface near infratemporal crest.
4. Perform zygomatic arch osteotomy or coronoidectomy if needed to pass muscle cleanly into maxilla/orbit.
pearls: Splitting the muscle sagittally allows transferring the anterior half while transposing the posterior half forward to eliminate temporal hollowing.
pitfalls: Injuring the frontal branch of the facial nerve by dissecting superficial to the deep temporal fascia fat pad.

recipient_vessels_options: Pedicled muscle flap on deep temporal arteries

references.book: Mathes SJ, Nahai F. Reconstructive Surgery: Principles, Anatomy, & Technique

name: Deltopectoral (Bakamjian) Flap

classification.cormack_lamberty: Type A axial fasciocutaneous (proximal) + random extension over deltoid

dominant_pedicle.artery: Internal mammary artery (IMA) perforators (2nd & 3rd intercostal spaces dominant)

minor_pedicles: Thoracoacromial cutaneous branches (divided during elevation — lateral portion becomes random-pattern)

perforators.label: 2nd & 3rd IMA Perforators
perforators.location: 1.5–2 cm lateral to sternal border in 2nd and 3rd intercostal spaces
perforators.relation_to_landmarks: 2nd ICS perforator is typically the largest axial contributor

vascular_anatomy.angiosome: Internal mammary angiosome (with choke capture of thoracoacromial/deltoid territory)
vascular_anatomy.venous_drainage_notes: Distal extension beyond the deltopectoral groove crosses choke vessels and carries high risk of distal necrosis without surgical delay.
vascular_variants: Prior sternotomy or CABG harvesting ipsilateral IMA is an absolute contraindication

dimensions.thickness_notes: Thin, pliable infraclavicular/deltoid skin; superior contour to pectoralis major for anterior neck resurfacing.

arc_of_rotation.pivot_point: Parasternal 2nd–3rd intercostal spaces (stop dissection ≥2 cm lateral to sternum)
arc_of_rotation.reach_description: Reaches anterior neck, tracheostoma, pharyngocutaneous fistulae, lower face, and upper sternum.

indications: Anterior neck resurfacing and tracheostoma/pharyngostoma closure
Salvage head & neck coverage when free flaps fail or recipient vessels depleted
Burn scar contracture release of anterior neck
contraindications: Ipsilateral IMA harvest (CABG) or prior sternotomy
Previous chest wall radiation across parasternal base
advantages: Thin, well-matched neck/lower face skin without muscle bulk
No microsurgery required
Preserves pectoralis major for potential concurrent or backup use
disadvantages: Donor site over deltoid/chest typically requires STSG
Often requires surgical delay (2–3 weeks) if extended lateral to deltopectoral groove
Two-stage pedicle division if tubed across intact neck skin

donor_site.closure: Split-thickness skin graft over deltoid/anterior chest defect (or partial primary closure medially).
morbidity: Mild nipple distortion if inferior border drops too low

technique.patient_positioning: Supine with ipsilateral shoulder slightly elevated.
preoperative_planning: Verify intact IMA (no prior LIMA/RIMA CABG)
Consider surgical delay 14–21 days prior if extending past deltopectoral groove
technique.design: Superior border along clavicle; inferior border parallel above anterior axillary fold and nipple; extend over deltoid as needed.
harvest_steps: 1. Elevate lateral-to-medial in subfascial plane (including deltoid and pectoral fascia).
2. Divide thoracoacromial cutaneous perforators at the deltopectoral groove carefully.
3. Stop medial dissection 2 cm lateral to sternal border to safeguard 2nd and 3rd IMA perforators.
4. Rotate superiorly into neck/lower face defect without kinking base; graft donor defect.
pearls: Never dissect closer than 2 cm to the sternal edge where IMA perforators emerge.
pitfalls: Extending over the lateral deltoid without prior surgical delay leads to distal tip necrosis.

recipient_vessels_options: Pedicled axial flap on IMA perforators
complications: Distal tip necrosis (up to 15–25% if undelayed)

references.book: Bakamjian VY. Plast Reconstr Surg (Deltopectoral Flap)

name: Lower / Lateral Trapezius Myocutaneous Flap

classification.mathes_nahai: Type II (transverse cervical / dorsal scapular dominant + occipital & intercostal minor)

dominant_pedicle.artery: Transverse cervical artery (superficial branch) and dorsal scapular artery (deep branch)
dominant_pedicle.veins: Transverse cervical vein (drains to external jugular or subclavian vein)

perforators.label: Lower Trapezius Musculocutaneous Perforators
perforators.location: Between vertebral border of scapula and spinous processes (T4–T10)
perforators.relation_to_landmarks: Dorsal scapular artery pierces rhomboid minor/major to supply lower trapezius

vascular_anatomy.venous_drainage_notes: Preserving both superficial descending transverse cervical and deep dorsal scapular branches maximizes safe paddle length below the scapular tip.
vascular_variants: Dorsal scapular artery arises directly from subclavian artery in ~70% of patients and passes through brachial plexus

motor: Spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) — preserve upper trapezius fibers to prevent shoulder droop

dimensions.thickness_notes: Thinner and more pliable than pectoralis major or latissimus dorsi for lateral skull base, occipital, and neck wounds.

arc_of_rotation.pivot_point: Posterior triangle of neck / medial border of levator scapulae
arc_of_rotation.reach_description: Reaches occiput, lateral skull base, auricle, posterior/lateral neck, upper thoracic spine, and shoulder.

indications: Occipital scalp and lateral skull base / temporal bone defects
Posterior neck and cervical spine hardware coverage
Salvage head & neck reconstruction outside prior anterior radiation fields
contraindications: Prior radical neck dissection with sacrifice of transverse cervical AND dorsal scapular vessels
advantages: Outside standard anterior neck radiation ports
Preserves shoulder elevation when upper trapezius and CN XI are spared
Primary donor closure up to 8–9 cm
disadvantages: Requires lateral decubitus or prone positioning
Variable transverse cervical vs dorsal scapular dominance

donor_site.closure: Primary vertical closure over suction drains.
morbidity: Shoulder droop if upper trapezius or CN XI is injured
donor_site.functional_loss: Minimal if upper fibers of trapezius and CN XI are preserved.

preoperative_planning: Verify prior neck dissection records for transverse cervical/dorsal scapular patency
Mark spinous processes, medial scapular border, and inferior scapular angle
landmarks: Medial border & inferior angle of scapula
technique.design: Vertical skin island centered between medial scapular border and midline, keeping ≥50% of paddle overlying trapezius muscle.
harvest_steps: 1. Incise lateral margin to identify lateral border of lower trapezius overlying latissimus dorsi.
2. Elevate lower trapezius off rhomboid major from inferior to superior.
3. Identify dorsal scapular artery emerging between rhomboid minor and major and preserve if maintaining deep supply (or divide rhomboid minor to lengthen arc).
4. Preserve upper trapezius fibers and spinal accessory nerve; tunnel into neck/occiput.
pearls: Keep at least half of the skin island directly over the lower trapezius muscle above the scapular tip for reliable perfusion.
pitfalls: Sacrificing the upper trapezius or CN XI causes debilitating winged scapula and shoulder drop.

recipient_vessels_options: Pedicled on transverse cervical / dorsal scapular vessels
complications: Distal skin tip necrosis (if designed too low below T12)

references.book: Netterville JL, Wood DE. Arch Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg (Lower Trapezius Flap)

name: Sternocleidomastoid (SCM) Muscle Flap

classification.mathes_nahai: Type II (occipital superiorly, superior thyroid middle, transverse cervical inferiorly)

tissue_components: Optional small overlying skin paddle (less reliable)

dominant_pedicle.artery: Occipital artery (superiorly based) and superior thyroid artery (middle segment)
dominant_pedicle.veins: Accompanying veins to internal jugular / external jugular system

vascular_anatomy.angiosome: Occipital / superior thyroid segmental neck angiosomes
vascular_anatomy.venous_drainage_notes: Muscle-only flap is markedly more reliable than myocutaneous version because skin perforators are tenuous.
vascular_variants: Segmental tripartite supply — preserve at least 2 of 3 pedicles when possible

motor: Spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) — enters posterior border; preserve carefully to avoid trapezius palsy
sensory: Great auricular nerve (superficial — preserve if possible)
nerves.donor_numbness_note: Ear lobule numbness if great auricular nerve is sacrificed.

dimensions.thickness_notes: Compact, well-vascularized muscle ideal for parotid bed contour, Frey syndrome prevention, and pharyngeal/esophageal reinforcement.

arc_of_rotation.pivot_point: Mastoid tip (superiorly based) or clavicle/sternum (inferiorly based)
arc_of_rotation.reach_description: Superiorly based fills parotidectomy bed, mastoid, floor of mouth, and mandible; inferiorly based reinforces tracheoesophageal / cervical esophageal repairs.

indications: Parotidectomy defect contour restoration & Frey syndrome prophylaxis
Carotid artery coverage after neck dissection
Cervical esophageal / tracheoesophageal fistula interposition
Floor of mouth / orocutaneous fistula reinforcement
contraindications: N+ ipsilateral neck requiring radical neck dissection
High-dose neck radiation with compromised segmental supply
advantages: Immediate proximity within existing neck/parotid incision
Minimal operative time (<30 min)
Effective interposition barrier for Frey syndrome and fistulae
disadvantages: Unreliable cutaneous paddle (high skin loss rate)
Risk to spinal accessory nerve
Mild neck contour asymmetry

donor_site.closure: Existing neck or parotidectomy incision closed primarily.
morbidity: Risk of CN XI traction injury

technique.patient_positioning: Supine with neck slightly extended and turned contralaterally.
preoperative_planning: Determine superiorly vs inferiorly based pivot
Plan preservation of CN XI
technique.design: Split or full-thickness muscle flap leaving either superior occipital or inferior clavicular pedicle intact.
harvest_steps: 1. Expose SCM through parotidectomy or transverse neck incision while protecting great auricular nerve.
2. Identify and protect spinal accessory nerve entering the deep/posterior aspect of upper-middle SCM.
3. Divide sternal and clavicular insertions (for superiorly based) or mastoid attachment (for inferiorly based).
4. Rotate muscle into parotid bed, over carotid sheath, or between trachea and esophagus.
pearls: Use as a muscle-only flap whenever possible; avoid relying on large SCM cutaneous paddles.
pitfalls: Transecting the spinal accessory nerve during superior mobilization causes trapezius paralysis.

references.book: Mathes SJ, Nahai F. Reconstructive Surgery: Principles, Anatomy, & Technique

name: Cervicofacial Advancement-Rotation Flap

dominant_pedicle.artery: Random subdermal plexus fed by facial, submental, and transverse cervical perforators

vascular_anatomy.venous_drainage_notes: Deep-plane (sub-SMAS / subplatysmal) dissection significantly enhances distal tip vascularity in smokers and large medial cheek defects.
vascular_variants: Heavy tobacco use substantially increases distal medial tip necrosis if raised subcutaneously

motor: Facial nerve branches (protected deep to parotidomasseteric fascia in subcutaneous plane; carefully visualized in deep plane)

dimensions.thickness_notes: Gold-standard facial color, hair, and texture match across the cheek aesthetic subunit.

arc_of_rotation.pivot_point: Inferior neck / retroauricular back-cut (extends to chest as cervicopectoral flap if needed)
arc_of_rotation.reach_description: Closes medium-to-large medial cheek, infraorbital, lateral nasal sidewall, and lower eyelid/malar defects.

indications: Medium-to-large cheek and infraorbital defects (>3–4 cm)
Lower eyelid / malar composite defects (Mustardé design)
Parotid-cheek cutaneous defects
contraindications: Active heavy smoking (strongly favor deep-plane dissection or alternative)
Prior preauricular/neck irradiation
advantages: Ideal like-for-like facial skin match
Scars hidden in lateral canthal, preauricular, hairline, and neck creases
Single-stage outpatient or short-stay procedure
disadvantages: Risk of lower eyelid ectropion if tension is directed inferiorly
Distal medial tip necrosis in smokers
Facial nerve injury risk in deep-plane dissection

donor_site.closure: Primary tension-free closure along preauricular and cervical incisions with standing-cone excision in nasolabial fold.
morbidity: Ectropion if not anchored to lateral orbital rim periosteum
donor_site.functional_loss: None when facial nerve and lower lid support are preserved.

preoperative_planning: Draw incision curving HIGH superiorly above lateral canthus (Mustardé arc) to prevent lower lid ectropion
Decide subcutaneous vs deep-plane (sub-SMAS) based on smoking history
technique.design: Carry superior limb superolaterally above lateral canthus toward temporal hairline, then down preauricular crease and into upper neck crease.
harvest_steps: 1. Incise along superolateral Mustardé arc, preauricular crease, and cervical extension.
2. Elevate in subcutaneous plane (or sub-SMAS / subplatysmal in smokers) protecting facial nerve branches.
3. Rotate superomedially and suspend dermal/SMAS layer firmly to lateral orbital rim periosteum.
4. Excise inferior standing cone along nasolabial fold and close without vertical tension on lower eyelid.
pearls: Always arc the superior incision ABOVE the lateral canthus and suture-anchor the flap to the lateral orbital rim periosteum to prevent ectropion.
pitfalls: Directing closing tension vertically downward on the lower eyelid causes severe cicatricial ectropion.

references.book: Baker SR. Local Flaps in Facial Reconstruction

name: Abbé–Estlander & Karapandzic Lip Flaps

dominant_pedicle.artery: Superior or inferior labial artery (courses in submucosal plane ~5–10 mm from free vermilion margin)

vascular_anatomy.venous_drainage_notes: Preserving a 5–7 mm vermilion/mucosal pedicle bridge safeguards the labial artery and accompanying veins.
vascular_variants: Labial artery lies deep to orbicularis oris (between muscle and mucosa) at level of vermilion-cutaneous junction

motor: Buccal & marginal mandibular facial nerve twigs (preserved intact in Karapandzic; divided/reinnervated in Abbé)
sensory: Infraorbital / mental nerve branches (preserved in Karapandzic)
nerves.donor_numbness_note: Karapandzic preserves immediate sensation and oral competence; Abbé regains partial sensation over 6–12 months.

dimensions.thickness_notes: True 3-layer composite lip reconstruction (skin, functional orbicularis sphincter, mucosa) designed at 1/2 the width of the defect.

arc_of_rotation.pivot_point: Labial artery at vermilion border (Abbé/Estlander) or bilateral commissures (Karapandzic)
arc_of_rotation.reach_description: Reconstructs 30–80% full-thickness central or lateral upper/lower lip defects while sharing loss evenly across both lips.

indications: Full-thickness lip defects involving 35–65% of lip width (Abbé for central/paracentral, Estlander for commissure)
Large lower lip defects 50–80% requiring immediate dynamic oral competence (Karapandzic)
Bilateral cleft lip whistle/philtral tight upper lip reconstruction (Abbé)
contraindications: Patients unable to tolerate 2–3 week cross-lip pedicle bridge (Abbé) or microstomia (Karapandzic)
advantages: Restores exact vermilion white roll, mucosa, and functional orbicularis oris sphincter
Balances upper and lower lip width evenly
disadvantages: Abbé requires 2-stage pedicle division at 14–21 days
Estlander blunts oral commissure (often needs secondary commissuroplasty)
Karapandzic risks microstomia in >75% lip defects

donor_site.closure: Precise 3-layer primary closure aligning vermilion-cutaneous white roll.
donor_site.functional_loss: Minimal; preserves oral competence and speech.

preoperative_planning: Design Abbé/Estlander width equal to 50% of defect width (height matches defect)
Tattoo vermilion white roll before local anesthetic injection
landmarks: Labial artery (~5–8 mm deep to mucosa)
technique.design: Full-thickness wedge/shield on opposite lip (half defect width) hinged on labial artery; or circumoral Karapandzic neurovascular advancement.
harvest_steps: 1. Mark white roll precisely before infiltration.
2. Incise full-thickness lip on non-pedicle side completely; stop 5–7 mm short of vermilion on pedicle side.
3. Rotate 180° across oral aperture and perform meticulous 3-layer closure (mucosa, orbicularis, skin).
4. Divide cross-lip pedicle and inset vermilion cleanly at 14–21 days (Abbé); Estlander is single-stage.
pearls: Design the cross-lip flap width at HALF the defect width so upper and lower lips end up symmetrical.
pitfalls: Misaligning the vermilion white roll by even 1 mm creates an obvious step-off deformity.

references.book: Baker SR. Local Flaps in Facial Reconstruction

name: Free Jejunal Visceral Flap

dominant_pedicle.veins: Single paired jejunal mesenteric vein (larger caliber)

vascular_anatomy.venous_drainage_notes: Thin-walled, friable mesenteric vein requires delicate handling; extremely short warm ischemia tolerance (~1–2 hours max).
vascular_variants: Transilluminate mesentery intraoperatively to select a long single-pedicle arcade

dimensions.thickness_notes: Pre-formed mucinous conduit matching circumferential pharyngoesophageal lumen diameter (~3–4 cm).

arc_of_rotation.reach_description: Circumferential pharyngoesophageal conduit from oropharynx to thoracic inlet.

indications: Circumferential total laryngopharyngectomy defects
Salvage pharyngoesophageal stricture or fistula
Mucosal resurfacing (opened jejunal patch)
contraindications: Severe mesenteric atherosclerosis or prior extensive small bowel resection
Inability to tolerate laparotomy/laparoscopy
advantages: Pre-tubularized lubricated mucosal conduit with lowest stricture rate
Low early pharyngocutaneous fistula rate
Can exteriorize a small sentinel monitoring loop
disadvantages: Requires abdominal entry (laparotomy/laparoscopic harvest)
Very low ischemia tolerance (<2 hours)
Wet/gurgly tracheoesophageal voice quality compared to tubed ALT/RFFF

donor_site.closure: End-to-end jejunojejunostomy and abdominal wall closure.
donor_site.functional_loss: None after uncomplicated small bowel anastomosis.

technique.patient_positioning: Supine (simultaneous two-team head & neck and abdominal harvest).
preoperative_planning: Coordinate general surgery team for laparotomy or laparoscopic harvest
Prepare neck recipient vessels BEFORE dividing mesenteric pedicle to minimize ischemia time
technique.design: 12–20 cm isoperistaltic jejunal segment plus optional 3 cm sentinel exteriorized monitoring loop on same arcade.
harvest_steps: 1. Prepare cervical recipient vessels completely before pedicle division.
2. Transilluminate mesentery 20–40 cm distal to ligament of Treitz to isolate single long arcade.
3. Mark proximal end with silk suture to guarantee isoperistaltic orientation in neck.
4. Perform revascularization FIRST (or rapid inset + microanastomosis) to keep ischemia <90 minutes; complete pharyngeal and esophageal anastomoses.
pearls: Always mark proximal end to ensure isoperistaltic inset and complete microvascular anastomosis promptly because mucosa sloughs rapidly after 2 hours of warm ischemia.
pitfalls: Anti-peristaltic inset causes severe dysphagia; redundant bowel length causes kinking and stasis.

recipient_vessels_options: Superior thyroid / facial / transverse cervical artery

references.book: Wei FC, Mardini S. Flaps and Reconstructive Surgery

name: Serratus Anterior Muscle / Osteomuscular Flap

classification.mathes_nahai: Type III (lateral thoracic artery + serratus branch of thoracodorsal artery)

tissue_components: Lower 3–4 slips of serratus anterior muscle

dominant_pedicle.artery: Serratus branch of thoracodorsal artery (subscapular system)

vascular_anatomy.venous_drainage_notes: Shares the subscapular vascular tree with latissimus dorsi and parascapular flaps for massive mega/chimeric reconstructions.
vascular_variants: 1–3 serratus branches arise from thoracodorsal artery; occasionally direct from subscapular trunk

motor: Long thoracic nerve (C5–C7) — preserve superior slips to prevent scapular winging

dimensions.thickness_notes: Thin, malleable, digitated muscle slips (lower 3–4 slips: ~8 × 12 cm) ideal for contoured extremity, facial reanimation, or intrathoracic coverage.

arc_of_rotation.reach_description: Pedicled to axilla, chest wall, intrathoracic bronchial stump/empyema; free flap for hand/foot dorsum, scalp, mandible/rib, and multi-vector facial reanimation.

indications: Thin contoured muscle + STSG for hand/wrist and foot/ankle defects
Intrathoracic bronchial stump reinforcement / empyema obliteration
Chimeric subscapular-system reconstruction with LD/scapular flaps
Vascularized rib + muscle for orbital/mandibular defects
contraindications: Harvesting upper 5 slips (causes severe winged scapula)
Prior axillary dissection dividing thoracodorsal pedicle
advantages: Exceptionally long, large-caliber pedicle (up to 16 cm)
Thin, flat muscle slips conform cleanly to irregular contours
Independent muscular slips allow multi-vector dynamic facial reanimation
disadvantages: Risk of scapular winging if >4 lower slips or upper long thoracic nerve is damaged
Lateral decubitus positioning
Risk of pneumothorax if rib is harvested

donor_site.closure: Primary closure over drain along midaxillary line.
morbidity: Scapular winging (if upper slips or long thoracic nerve violated)
donor_site.functional_loss: Negligible if only the lowest 3–4 slips are harvested.

preoperative_planning: Limit harvest strictly to lowest 3–4 slips (ribs 6–9) to avoid scapular winging
Plan subscapular chimeric harvest if large combined defect
technique.design: Midaxillary curvilinear incision exposing anterior border of latissimus dorsi and serratus slips.
harvest_steps: 1. Retract anterior border of latissimus dorsi posteriorly to expose thoracodorsal pedicle and serratus branch.
2. Trace long thoracic nerve along superficial surface of serratus; preserve branches to upper 5–6 slips.
3. Divide lowest 3–4 muscular slips off ribs 6–9 and scapular tip (leave intercostal fascia intact to avoid pneumothorax).
4. Trace serratus branch proximally onto thoracodorsal / subscapular vessels for maximum length.
pearls: Restricting harvest to the lower 3 slips while keeping the upper long thoracic nerve intact prevents scapular winging.
pitfalls: Violating parietal pleura during periosteal rib elevation.

references.book: Wei FC, Mardini S. Flaps and Reconstructive Surgery

name: Inferior Gluteal Artery Perforator (IGAP) Flap

dominant_pedicle.artery_origin: Anterior division of internal iliac artery

perforators.label: Inferior Gluteal Perforators
perforators.location: Inferior half of buttock, 1–5 cm above inferior gluteal crease
perforators.relation_to_landmarks: Emerge inferior to piriformis near line from PSIS to ischial tuberosity

vascular_anatomy.venous_drainage_notes: Slightly longer pedicle than SGAP (7–11 cm) because vessels course obliquely through lower gluteus maximus.
vascular_variants: Close proximity to sciatic nerve and posterior femoral cutaneous nerve

motor: Sciatic nerve (lies deep to piriformis — preserve)
sensory: Posterior femoral cutaneous nerve (can harvest for sensate breast or preserve to avoid sitting paresthesia)
nerves.donor_numbness_note: Posterior thigh/gluteal sensory change; sitting discomfort if ischial fat pad is over-resected.

dimensions.thickness_notes: Firm, projection-holding gluteal fat; scar concealed in the inferior gluteal crease (unlike SGAP).

arc_of_rotation.reach_description: Pedicled for ischial pressure injuries and perineal defects; free flap for autologous breast reconstruction.

indications: Secondary autologous breast reconstruction when DIEP is unavailable
Ischial pressure injury coverage (pedicled propeller / V-Y IGAP)
Perineal / vulvovaginal reconstruction
contraindications: Prior gluteal liposuction or silicone injections
Chronic sciatic neuropathy
advantages: Well-concealed scar in inferior gluteal crease
Longer pedicle than SGAP
Spares gluteus maximus muscle
disadvantages: Requires intraoperative prone-to-supine position change for breast reconstruction
Risk of sitting pain over ischial tuberosity if deep ischial fat pad is removed
Sciatic nerve proximity

donor_site.closure: Primary layered closure in inferior gluteal fold; preserve fat pad directly over ischial tuberosity.
donor_site.functional_loss: None when gluteus maximus is spared.

technique.patient_positioning: Prone for harvest; reposition supine for breast inset.
preoperative_planning: Preoperative CTA to map dominant IGA perforators
Mark inferior gluteal fold standing to conceal scar
technique.design: Oblique ellipse parallel to and ~1 cm above inferior gluteal crease; bevel superiorly, NOT over ischial tuberosity.
harvest_steps: 1. Elevate subfascially from lateral to medial identifying dominant IGA perforators.
2. Split lower gluteus maximus fibers carefully following perforator toward IGA trunk.
3. Identify and protect sciatic nerve and posterior femoral cutaneous nerve.
4. Leave generous fat pad over ischial tuberosity and close over drains.
pearls: Preserve the protective fat pad directly overlying the ischial tuberosity to prevent chronic postoperative sitting pain.
pitfalls: Aggressive medial inferior beveling exposes the ischial tuberosity and causes painful sitting.

references.book: Blondeel PN et al. Perforator Flaps: Anatomy, Technique, & Clinical Applications

name: Lumbar Artery Perforator (LAP) Flap

dominant_pedicle.veins: Lumbar perforating vein (often requires composite DIEV/thoracodorsal interposition graft for breast)

perforators.label: 4th Lumbar Perforator
perforators.location: 7–9 cm lateral to posterior midline, just superior to posterior iliac crest
perforators.relation_to_landmarks: Pierces thoracolumbar fascia between erector spinae and quadratus lumborum

vascular_anatomy.venous_drainage_notes: Short native pedicle (4–6 cm) usually mandates a composite arteriovenous interposition graft (commonly deep inferior epigastric vessels) for free breast transfer.
vascular_variants: 4th lumbar perforator is most consistent for breast volume; verify exact level on preoperative CTA

sensory: Superior cluneal nerves (can be coapted for sensate breast reconstruction)
nerves.donor_numbness_note: Upper buttock/flank numbness; waist-contouring aesthetic donor site.

dimensions.thickness_notes: Soft, natural breast-like flank fat that improves waist contour (body-lift effect).

arc_of_rotation.pivot_point: Lateral border of erector spinae / thoracolumbar fascia
arc_of_rotation.reach_description: Pedicled for lumbosacral spine defects; free flap (with composite AV graft) for autologous breast reconstruction.

indications: Autologous breast reconstruction in thin patients lacking abdominal tissue
Lumbosacral spine wound / hardware coverage (pedicled propeller LAP)
contraindications: Prior extensive posterior flank liposuction
Inability to perform composite vascular interposition graft
advantages: Natural soft breast tissue consistency
Favorable waist/flank donor contour
Preserves rectus, gluteal, and back muscles
disadvantages: Short pedicle (4–6 cm) almost always requiring AV interposition graft
High technical difficulty and prone-to-supine position change
High donor seroma rate

donor_site.closure: Primary layered closure with progressive tension sutures and closed suction drains.

technique.patient_positioning: Prone for harvest; supine for breast microanastomosis (plus DIEV interposition graft harvest).
preoperative_planning: Preoperative CTA essential to localize dominant L3/L4 perforator
Plan composite DIEV or thoracodorsal vascular graft
technique.design: Oblique fusiform paddle over flank / upper buttock centered on L4 perforator (~8 cm from midline).
harvest_steps: 1. Harvest composite arteriovenous interposition graft (e.g., DIEA/V) while supine if performing breast transfer.
2. Prone: elevate lateral-to-medial over gluteal/thoracolumbar fascia toward lateral erector spinae border.
3. Dissect L4 perforator through thoracolumbar fascia between erector spinae and quadratus lumborum.
4. Divide pedicle, close flank with progressive tension sutures, reposition supine, and anastomose via interposition graft.
pearls: Harvesting a composite deep inferior epigastric AV graft solves both the short pedicle length and small arterial caliber mismatch.
pitfalls: High seroma rate if quilting/progressive tension sutures are omitted.

recipient_vessels_options: Internal mammary vessels via DIEA/V interposition graft

references.book: Opsomer D et al. Plast Reconstr Surg (LAP Flap for Breast Reconstruction)

name: Greater Omental (Gastroepiploic) Visceral Flap

dominant_pedicle.artery: Right gastroepiploic artery (dominant — larger caliber) and left gastroepiploic artery
dominant_pedicle.veins: Right gastroepiploic vein (drains to superior mesenteric / gastrocolic trunk)

vascular_anatomy.venous_drainage_notes: Preserving the main gastroepiploic arch and dividing short gastric branches allows dramatic pedicle lengthening.
vascular_variants: Right gastroepiploic artery is typically larger and preferred for pedicled sternal/pelvic or free transfer

nerves.donor_numbness_note: Laparoscopic or upper midline laparotomy incisions.

dimensions.thickness_notes: Exceptionally malleable vascular-immunologic apron (~20 × 30 cm unfolded); conforms into deep sternal, mediastinal, skull base, or chronic osteomyelitis cavities.

arc_of_rotation.pivot_point: Pylorus / right gastroepiploic origin (or splenic hilum for left)
arc_of_rotation.reach_description: Pedicled via diaphragmatic/subxiphoid tunnel to mediastinum, sternum, chest wall, breast, neck, or pelvis; free flap for scalp, extremity osteomyelitis, and vascularized lymph node transfer (VLNT).

indications: Deep sternal wound infection / mediastinitis & infected vascular grafts (gold-standard salvage)
Radionecrotic chest wall or pelvic cavity obliteration
Vascularized lymph node transfer (VLNT) for lymphedema
Large scalp / cranial osteomyelitis defects (+ STSG)
contraindications: Prior total omentectomy or extensive gastrectomy dividing gastroepiploic arch
Severe intra-abdominal carcinomatosis/adhesions
advantages: Unmatched immunologic/angiogenic resistance in infected or irradiated beds
Long reach and extreme malleability
Laparoscopic harvest minimizes abdominal morbidity
disadvantages: Requires peritoneal entry
Requires STSG for surface coverage
Risk of epigastric/diaphragmatic tunnel hernia

donor_site.closure: Laparoscopic port closure or midline fascial closure leaving loose tunnel without strangulating pedicle.

preoperative_planning: Review prior abdominal surgical history
Consider laparoscopic harvest to reduce hernia/ileus risk
technique.design: Detach omentum from transverse colon along avascular plane, divide left gastroepiploic and short gastric branches while preserving right gastroepiploic arcade.
harvest_steps: 1. Enter abdomen (laparoscopically or via upper midline laparotomy) and inspect omental volume and arch.
2. Separate greater omentum off transverse colon in avascular plane.
3. Ligate left gastroepiploic vessels and serial gastric branches close to greater curvature to preserve Barkow arcade.
4. Deliver pedicled omentum through subxiphoid fascial tunnel (2–3 fingerbreadths) into mediastinum/chest without twist, or divide right gastroepiploic pedicle for free transfer.
pearls: Laparoscopic omental harvest avoids a full laparotomy while preserving full pedicle length for sternal or breast coverage.
pitfalls: Creating an overly tight subxiphoid fascial tunnel causes pedicle venous congestion; overly wide tunnel causes epigastric hernia.

references.book: Zenn MR, Jones G. Reconstructive Surgery: Anatomy, Technique, and Clinical Applications

name: External Oblique Musculofascial / Myocutaneous Flap

classification.mathes_nahai: Type IV (segmental lower 8 posterior intercostal arteries)

dominant_pedicle.artery: Segmental posterior intercostal arteries (T5–T12) and deep circumflex iliac branches

vascular_anatomy.venous_drainage_notes: Preserving lateral/posterior segmental intercostal entries allows wide medial and superior advancement.
vascular_variants: Release along linea semilunaris yields 5–10 cm per side of midline advancement in Ramirez components separation

motor: Lower thoracic intercostal nerves (T7–T12) — enter posteriorly; stay superficial to internal oblique

dimensions.thickness_notes: Broad, durable musculofascial sheet providing dynamic innervated abdominal wall or lower chest wall coverage.

arc_of_rotation.reach_description: Advances medially for complex ventral hernias (components separation) or rotates superiorly up to inframammary / lower chest wall (4th rib).

indications: Complex midline ventral hernia repair (Ramirez anterior components separation)
Large lower chest wall / mastectomy / chest-wall radionecrosis defects
Upper abdominal wall full-thickness defects
contraindications: Prior extensive lateral abdominal wall transection (e.g., chevron/subcostal + flank incisions dividing segmental supply)
advantages: Restores dynamic, autologous abdominal wall continuity
Huge surface area for chest wall salvage without microsurgery
Preserves rectus abdominis
disadvantages: Risk of lateral abdominal bulge if internal oblique/transversus abdominis is violated
Skin undermining in open components separation increases seroma/wound breakdown

donor_site.closure: Primary closure (perforator-sparing components separation reduces wound morbidity); mesh reinforcement if needed.
morbidity: Lateral bulge if internal oblique is injured
donor_site.functional_loss: Minimal when internal oblique and transversus abdominis remain intact.

preoperative_planning: Review abdominal CT for prior ostomies, incisions, and fascial defect width
Consider perforator-sparing tunnels to preserve periumbilical DIEA skin supply
technique.design: Incise external oblique aponeurosis 1–2 cm lateral to linea semilunaris from costal margin to inguinal ligament.
harvest_steps: 1. Expose external oblique aponeurosis lateral to linea semilunaris (preserving periumbilical perforators if possible).
2. Incise external oblique aponeurosis longitudinally 1.5–2 cm lateral to rectus sheath.
3. Develop avascular plane between external oblique and internal oblique laterally to midaxillary line.
4. Advance musculofascial complex medially (or rotate composite myocutaneous flap superiorly onto chest wall).
pearls: Staying 1.5–2 cm lateral to the linea semilunaris prevents inadvertent entry into the rectus sheath or injury to the neurovascular bundle on the surface of transversus abdominis.
pitfalls: Violating the internal oblique fascia creates a difficult-to-repair lateral Spigelian-type hernia.

references.book: Mathes SJ, Nahai F. Reconstructive Surgery: Principles, Anatomy, & Technique

name: Paraspinous Muscle Turnover / Advancement Flap

classification.mathes_nahai: Type IV (segmental posterior intercostal & lumbar medial/lateral branches)

dominant_pedicle.artery: Segmental medial and lateral branches of posterior intercostal (thoracic) and lumbar arteries

vascular_anatomy.venous_drainage_notes: Medial branches enter near transverse processes (preserved in medial advancement); lateral branches enter laterally (preserved in turnover/bipedicled advancement).
vascular_variants: Extensive spine hardware dissection often disrupts medial branches — rely on lateral segmental supply when mobilizing bilaterally

motor: Posterior primary rami of spinal nerves

dimensions.thickness_notes: Thick, well-vascularized bilateral paravertebral muscle columns ideal for obliterating deep midline spine dead space over hardware.

arc_of_rotation.pivot_point: Bipedicled medial advancement (lateral fascial release) or medial/lateral turnover
arc_of_rotation.reach_description: Covers exposed cervical, thoracic, and lumbar spinal hardware and dural repairs directly along the posterior midline.

indications: Prophylactic or salvage coverage of exposed thoracic/lumbar spinal instrumentation
Post-laminectomy wound dehiscence and CSF leak reinforcement
Irradiated spinal oncology defects
contraindications: Severe muscle atrophy/destruction from massive tumor resection or infection
Very wide (>8–10 cm) cutaneous defects requiring additional latissimus/trapezius/perforator flap
advantages: Direct in-situ exposure through existing spine incision
Preserves shoulder and extremity function
High hardware-salvage rate in complex spine surgery
disadvantages: Limited lateral reach (<6–8 cm width)
High seroma risk without obliteration and prolonged drains

donor_site.closure: Tension-free midline myofascial and skin closure over deep + subcutaneous drains.
morbidity: Wound dehiscence if skin closed under tension
donor_site.functional_loss: Minimal postural impact beyond underlying spine fusion.

preoperative_planning: Determine whether medial pedicles were disrupted by spine exposure
Have latissimus dorsi or trapezius ready as backup for large/irradiated defects
technique.design: Bilateral bipedicled paraspinous muscle advancement with longitudinal lateral fascial release.
harvest_steps: 1. Debride necrotic soft tissue and irrigate exposed spinal instrumentation thoroughly.
2. Elevate subcutaneous skin flaps laterally just beyond lateral border of paraspinous muscles.
3. Release thoracolumbar fascia longitudinally lateral to erector spinae and elevate muscle off ribs/transverse processes preserving lateral segmental pedicles.
4. Advance bilateral muscle columns medially over hardware and suture together in midline without tension over closed suction drains.
pearls: A bilateral longitudinal release of the lateral thoracolumbar fascia adds 3–5 cm of tension-free medial advancement over bulky pedicle screws.
pitfalls: Attempting to close tight irradiated midline skin directly over hardware without muscle interposition.

references.book: Mericli AF et al. Plast Reconstr Surg (Complex Spine Reconstruction)
